paras: The Center Point riots were a series of armed clashes between Black and white men at Center Point, Howard County, Arkansas, in late August 1881. Dispatches from Little Rock reported that Black men, and in one account a white man, were killed, though they disagreed on the toll. The fullest account traced one battle to the beating of a Black man, Anderson Smith, by two white men, and the story ran in weekly papers across the Midwest.

According to the Little Rock telegram, "the worst feeling imaginable" prevailed between Black and white residents of Center Point, and several riots had already occurred with loss of life. Center Point lay off the telegraph line, which the telegram gave as the reason its particulars were meager.

On a Monday, Smith, described as a "well-to-do negro," came into town, became intoxicated and was "roughly handled by two white men." The next day he returned with thirty or forty Black men, and a body of white men met them on the outskirts of town. In what the telegram called a regular battle, the Black men were driven into a barn and, after several hours, retreated to the woods, and several were killed.

Two other Little Rock dispatches described clashes without naming anyone. A special to the Memphis Appeal dated August 31 reported "another riot" two days earlier in which one Black man was killed and two white men were badly wounded. A National Associated Press report dated September 1 told of a pitched battle the previous Saturday at "Central Point" in which two Black men and one white man died.

The telegram reported that Black residents had "repeatedly threatened to burn the town," which was being guarded day and night. No report of arrests, an inquest or prosecutions appears in the coverage, and the dead were not named.

Coverage came entirely from brief Little Rock wire items in the white press. The Memphis Appeal gave the riot two sentences at the end of a Little Rock special on a murder arrest. The Omaha Daily Bee headed its item "SANGUINARY RIOT" and "Pitched Battle Between Blacks and Whites in Arkansas," and its dispatch dismissed everyone involved as "roughs."

The longer telegram naming Smith ran on September 8 and 9 in the Crawford Avalanche of Michigan, the Iowa Plain Dealer, the True Northerner of Michigan and the Kenosha Telegraph of Wisconsin. These papers placed it among crime briefs and weekly news summaries, and the text closed on Black threats to burn the town rather than on the dead.

The dispatches disagree on the day and the toll: about August 29 with one Black man dead and two white men wounded, a Saturday with two Black men and one white man dead, or a Tuesday with "several" killed. Because each said several riots had occurred, they may describe separate clashes rather than one battle.

reader.title: Center Point riots (1881)
bases: The dispatches describe repeated riots and at least one armed battle between bodies of Black and white men at Center Point, with Black men driven into a barn and killed (A1, A3, A6).

Three separate Little Rock dispatches (a Memphis Appeal special, a National Associated Press report and an undated telegram) agree that racial riots with deaths occurred at Center Point, Howard County, though they differ on the day and the toll, and only the telegram names Anderson Smith (A1, A3, A6).
